stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Astronomers at a high-altitude observatory spent three clear nights tracking a faint comet as it swung toward the Sun, measuring how quickly its tail lengthened. On the fourth night, a bank of clouds settled over the mountain ______ team used the lost observing time to recalibrate the telescope's camera and check the previous nights' measurements for errors.
explanation: "On the fourth night, a bank of clouds settled over the mountain" can stand alone as a sentence, and so can "the team used the lost observing time to recalibrate..." When two complete sentences meet, a semicolon is one of the correct ways to join them, so you should pick the semicolon.

A.why: You went with the comma because the break sounds like a short pause. But both sides are complete sentences, and a comma alone can't join two sentences. This is a comma splice.

C.why: You left out the punctuation, which runs two complete sentences together into a run-on. A boundary is needed between "mountain" and "the team."

D.why: You saw that "and" can join two sentences, but a FANBOYS word between two complete sentences needs a comma in front of it. Without the comma, this is still a run-on.

subtype_name: Run-on / comma splice: join or split two full sentences

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In traditional Japanese woodblock printing, the artist's design was transferred to several blocks of cherry wood, and a separate block was carved for every color. A single landscape print might require a dozen of these ______ one had to line up exactly with the others, or the colors would overlap and blur the image's fine edges.
explanation: "A single landscape print might require a dozen of these blocks" is a complete sentence. "Each one had to line up exactly with the others..." is also a complete sentence. A comma plus the FANBOYS word "and" is a correct way to join two sentences, so this is the answer.

A.why: You treated "each one had to line up..." as a description of the blocks. But it has its own subject ("each one") and verb ("had"), so it's a full sentence. Joining it to another sentence with only a comma makes a comma splice.

B.why: With no punctuation, the two complete sentences fuse into a run-on. You need a boundary between "blocks" and "each."

D.why: You knew a comma and "and" belonged together, but you put the comma on the wrong side. It has to come before the conjunction. Here it lands after "and," so it doesn't mark the boundary between the two sentences.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: To prepare for a regional measles vaccination drive, a district health office trained nearly two hundred community health workers. Those workers visited more than four thousand rural households over the course of the six-week ______ door to door, they logged each child's immunization history on a shared tablet so that clinics could identify any doses that had been missed.
explanation: "Those workers visited more than four thousand rural households over the course of the six-week campaign" is a complete sentence. What follows also has its own subject and verb ("they logged"), so it is a second complete sentence that happens to open with "Working door to door." A period correctly separates the two.

A.why: The participle "working" made the second half look like a modifier attached to the first sentence. Read on, though, and "they logged" shows it's a complete sentence. That makes this comma a comma splice.

B.why: With no punctuation, the first sentence runs straight into the second, which creates a run-on. You need a full stop before "Working."

C.why: You tried to join the two sentences with "and" but left out the comma that has to come before it, so the result is still a run-on. Inserting "and" also makes "working door to door" read awkwardly as if it continued the first clause.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: After the body fights off an infection, most of the immune cells that attacked the invader die within a few weeks. A small population of memory B cells, however, can survive in the bone marrow for decades after the ______ long lifespan allows the immune system to produce antibodies within days, rather than weeks, if the same pathogen ever returns.
explanation: "A small population of memory B cells, however, can survive in the bone marrow for decades after the infection" is a complete sentence. "This long lifespan allows the immune system to produce antibodies..." is a complete sentence too. A semicolon is a correct way to join two complete sentences.

B.why: The two ideas are closely related, so a comma felt like enough. A comma alone still can't join two complete sentences, however closely linked they are. This is a comma splice.

C.why: Leaving out the punctuation fuses two complete sentences into a run-on. You need a boundary before "this."

D.why: "And" can join two sentences only if a comma comes before it. Without that comma, this choice is still a run-on.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Sea otters along the Pacific coast often rest in groups, called rafts, that float just beyond the breaking waves. Before dozing off, an otter will roll over several times to wrap itself in strands of giant kelp that are anchored to the seafloor. Researchers believe the animals do this to stay in place while they ______ keeps them from drifting out of their feeding grounds on the tide.
explanation: "Researchers believe the animals do this to stay in place while they sleep" is a complete sentence. "The kelp keeps them from drifting out of their feeding grounds on the tide" is another one. A period correctly separates them.

A.why: A comma seemed like a natural pause after "sleep," but there is a complete sentence on each side. A bare comma between them is a comma splice.

B.why: With no punctuation, the reader can't tell where the first sentence ends, and the two complete sentences fuse into a run-on.

D.why: You treated "then" as a joining word. It isn't a FANBOYS conjunction, though, so a comma plus "then" still can't join two complete sentences. This is still a comma splice.
